newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian finance minister hopeful after budget blow.
newsitem.headline: Russian finance minister hopeful after budget blow.

text.p: Russian Finance Minister Alexander Livshits said on Saturday he still hoped the government's 1997 budget would be passed by the end of this year, even though parliament rejected it at the first reading.

The State Duma lower house threw out the draft by 280 votes to 33 on Friday after representatives of every party and group in the chamber, including government supporters, spoke out against the plans.

Despite deputies' criticism that revenues and expenditure were unbalanced and that the measures outlined were inadequate to reactivate industrial and social policies, Livshits said he was hopeful of reaching a compromise.
"We want the budget ready by the end of the year as it should be and any delay in this will not help matters," Livshits told a news conference.
"The government is ready to take note of the deputies' opinions."
But he made clear the government was prepared to compromise only on some issues and that it would stick to its main targets.
The government would stick firmly to a deficit target of 3.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), he said.
The government proposed an austere budget to try to keep down inflation amd wants to stick to targets agreed with the International Monetary Fund.
An IMF delegation is due in Moscow next week to disccuss economic performance and whether to release the next tranche of a three-year $10 billion loan.

Deputies in the opposition-dominated Duma say the budget will not do enough to revive the recession-hit economy. They are mindful of millions of workers, including servicemen, who have not been paid for months under a payments crisis.
The Duma agreed on Friday to set up a working group which will discuss which of two alternatives to present to deputies next Wednesday, October 16. The group will meet on Monday.
One possibility is to reject the draft outright and order the government to produce a new one within 20 days.

Alternatively, the Duma can call for the formation of a tripartite conciliation commission, with representatives from the Duma, the Federation Council upper house and the government, to thrash out the differences.
